profile.campus: Espoo, Finland (Equinix HE7, registry name "Equinix Data Center"; part of Equinix's Helsinki-region cluster)
profile.reading:
This is Equinix's HE7 facility at Sinimaentie 8 in Espoo, Finland, part of a cluster of Equinix buildings, HE3 through HE7, that the company markets collectively under its Helsinki region heading even though several, including this one, sit in the neighboring city of Espoo rather than Helsinki proper. This row carries the generic registry name "Equinix Data Center" rather than a facility code, but its website field already pointed to Equinix's dedicated HE7 page, which describes the building as reinforced concrete with 1,450 square meters, about 15,608 square feet, of colocation space, N+1 power and cooling redundancy, generator autonomy of 30 hours or more at full load, and a 99.9999%-plus global uptime guarantee; it does not publish a specific IT capacity figure in megawatts or kilowatts. Equinix entered the European colocation market through its 2007 acquisition of IXEurope and expanded further through its 2015 acquisition of TelecityGroup for about $3.8 billion, though Equinix's current HE7 page does not attribute the building to either predecessor company by name. Equinix, founded in Silicon Valley in 1998, converted to a real estate investment trust in January 2015 and trades on Nasdaq as EQIX.

As an EU-based facility, this data center falls under the European Union's Energy Efficiency Directive reporting requirements, which since 2024 have required data centers above a minimum capacity threshold to report power usage effectiveness, water usage, and other sustainability metrics to a European Commission database, part of a broader EU push for standardized data center energy transparency that does not have a direct equivalent in most of the US markets covered elsewhere in this registry.

Finland has positioned itself as a Nordic data center hub in part due to its naturally cool climate, which reduces cooling energy costs, and its access to renewable hydro and wind power from the broader Nordic electricity grid; several other major operators beyond Equinix, including Google and Microsoft, have also built large-scale data centers in Finland citing similar climate and clean-power advantages.

reading.body:
Equinix operates a 15,608 square foot colocation facility in Espoo, Finland, with published redundancy specifications but no disclosed IT capacity in megawatts.

The facility's technical specifications emphasize reliability rather than scale. N plus 1 power and cooling redundancy, 30-hour generator autonomy at full load, and a 99.9999 percent uptime guarantee are standard commitments for Equinix properties. The reinforced concrete building structure supports these guarantees. However, the operator did not publish the megawatt capacity of this specific site, limiting what the data can say about how much compute it can actually support.

This Espoo facility is one of 11 European sites in the registry researched in this batch, part of Equinix's broader European presence. That presence traces to acquisitions, particularly the 2007 purchase of IXEurope and 2015 acquisition of TelecityGroup, though no specific lineage connects this building to either predecessor company. The data covers the facility's footprint and stated redundancy but does not establish how many customers it serves, what interconnections it houses, or how its power and cooling capacity translate to usable AI infrastructure. The absence of published megawatt figures across Equinix's facility pages in this research batch means facility-level capacity cannot be compared or aggregated into regional or global scaling estimates from these sources alone.
